newsitem.title: ARMENIA: NATO chief rejects Russian criticism of trip.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief rejects Russian criticism of trip.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, stung by Russian criticism of his trip to several ex-Soviet republics, on Wednesday defended his right to visit members of the alliance's Partnership for Peace programme.
Speaking to reporters after meeting Armenia's President Levon Ter-Petrosyan in the capital Yerevan, Solana said: "I have come to this country because the president invited me."

"These countries are part of the Partnership for Peace and I have to visit all of the countries of the PFP," he said. The PFP, of which Russia is also a member, is designed to forge closer ties between former Cold War foes.

Solana has been accused by Moscow of pursuing a hidden agenda during his trip, which also includes Moldova, Georgia and Azerbaijan. Russia, angry about NATO's plans to expand eastwards, regards these countries as its strategic underbelly.

"I don't see why a visit to these countries must be interpreted as a secret agenda of NATO. Our relationship with these countries does not mean that they have the same type of relations with Russia," a visibly agitated Solana said.
Earlier President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said Solana had "undeclared, behind-the-scenes" aims in making his tour of the four southern republics.

"The West as a whole, and the leadership of NATO in particular, is opposed to any form of political or military integration between the newly independent states -- the republics of the former USSR, especially when they are initiated by Moscow," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.
Georgia and Armenia still have Russian military bases on their soil and analysts say the West has never actively challenged Russia's continuing leading role in the tinderbox Caucasus region.

Wednesday's exchange points to new strains in ties between NATO and Russia over the alliance's plans to take in former Warsaw Pact member states from eastern and central Europe. Russia regards NATO's expansion as a threat to its own security.
Solana ends his trip on Thursday with a visit to Azerbaijan, embroiled with Armenia in an eight-year old territorial dispute.
